messages.subject: Re: Fwd: Re: Fwd: [DIST-SAMP] 3 sampling questions
parts:
>> >> I have successfully used Distance, with a mobile, truck-mounted marine
>> >> radar, to estimate nearshore seabird densities within a 0.5 nautical mile
>> >> radius semi-circular point transect area from beach shorelines using
>> >> multiple transect points.
> >
>> >> 1. I now wish to estimate seabird densities from an offshore platform. The
>> >> point transect samples will be from a single point in space, and vary only
>> >> in time, not both space and time. Typically, I expect to obtain distances
>> >> to 15 or 20 targets within a 3 to 4 minute period, using the radar track-
>> >> ball cursor. Beyond that, it is difficult to assure that a given target is
>> >> not being detected twice.
> >
>> >> I anticipate sampling at perhaps hourly intervals to estimate both diurnal
>> >> and noctural seabird densities at that single point in space. Would this
>> >> sampling design work within the Distance framework?

The problem with this is that you have only one sample point, whereas
Distance is intended to draw inference for a wider area, based on
representative sampling. So at best, you're estimating numbers passing in
a narrow belt centered on the platform.

>> >> 2. In addition to the standard horizontal radar rotation mentioned above,
>> >> I intend to flip the radar 90 degrees to a vertical rotation plane. The
>> >> purpose is to obtain an angle and a distance to a bird target in order to
>> >> calculate the height above water of the target. In effect, the radar has
>> >> established a vertical, semi-circular plane 0.5 nm in radius in order to
>> >> detect birds passing through the plane. Can this 1.0 nm distance at the
>> >> waterline be considered to be a line transect? The height of the bird
>> >> target above water would then be equivalent to the perpendicular distance
>> >> of the target to the transect line. Is this reasonable?

Not really, as the vertical distribution of birds will be non-uniform, so
you can't disentangle detectability and availability, except by jointly
modelling the distance and angle data - which can't currently be done in
Distance. If your birds were flying predomnantly in one direction, e.g.
during migration, you can conceptually freeze the birds in position, and
regard the platform as traversing a line transect - which would be
perpendicular to the line you're imagining. Then horizontal distances to
the platform would be the perpendicular distances. This would be a
sensible option if few birds pass too high to be detected.

>> >> 3. Distance assumes that all birds are detected at zero distance from a
>> >> point or line transect. But a radar beam is angular (typically about 22
>> >> degrees), spreading out with increasing distance from the survey point.
>> >> Thus no birds are detected at zero distance. How does one compensate for
>> >> this fact in Distance?

Point transects have exactly the same issue. Just specify a sampling
fraction of 22/360, and use point transect methods, if you're going to use
distances from the platform. but see the above comments for reasons why
this might not make sense.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 25d2ffb7b5f86e67
messages.subject: Re: Fwd: Re: Fwd: [DIST-SAMP] 3 sampling questions
parts:
Steve, thank you for your response.

In regards to question 1, sampling birds in a marine environment, I cannot use a laser rangefinder to determine the distance from observer to bird, as water absorbs the laser. A radar works very well to determine the distance. So, theoretically, if the radar is mounted on a mobile boat, I can do either line transects, or point transects if the boat is moved to various positions. But there is no way to use Distance from a single, stationary observation point. On land, the resources (habitat, food sources) are stationary and the birds move between them. Over water, the resources are mobile. For example, schools of fishes, the prey, are constantly moving. Birds, as predators of the fish, may be more or less randomly distributed as they search for fish, and watch other birds, but as soon as a school is detected the birds aggregate. In addition, the water mass itself is constantly moving. If I observe birds at some time interval, it is unlikely that I am observing the same
birds. If I throw a bucket over to sample the water, I am not sampling the same water. So, while the observation point is static, the environment is dynamic. What is a reasonable time interval to consider the samples independent?

In regards to question 2, sampling a vertical plane, I know that the birds will not be uniformly distributed. Most of them will be at lower heights above the water. I see why that will not work.

For question 3, the 22 degrees is the vertical angle, so 22/360 will not work. The probability of detecting a bird increases with distance, out to a certain point where the reflected signal is too weak to be detected, because the area covered by the beam increases in both height and breadth. It is this inability to detect a bird close to the observer that bothers me. It is assumed that all birds at zero distance are detected, when, in fact, none are.

I am trying to design a study for a proposed offshore wind farm. Initially, there will be one meteorological tower where I can mount a radar. Eventually there may be two towers. Pending estimates of bird-rotor collision mortality the area may be populated with wind turbines. But if Distance cannot be used to estimate bird density from just one or two sampling points, there would appear to be little reason to install radars on the towers. Do you have any thoughts on this sampling problem?

Bob McFarlane
